paras: The attempted lynching of Ben Scott took place in Elkhart, Indiana, in August 1888, after Scott was accused of stabbing three men there on August 3. A posse formed to lynch him missed the officers who took him to the jail at Goshen, and after one of the stabbed men, Cornelius Crowley, died on August 6 there was renewed talk of a lynching party. No attack on the jail is reported, and Scott remained in custody.

Scott, about forty-five, was described as a wealthy Texan who had come to Elkhart a few weeks earlier to look after property he owned behind the Clifton House. According to the Indianapolis Journal's Elkhart correspondent, he had quarreled with neighbors he accused of trespassing and had said he would do some stabbing. Later reports gave his home as Columbus, Missouri, where he had four children and a brother.

On the afternoon of August 3, in an alley near Crowley's barn, Scott was said to have stabbed Crowley, a young stock dealer, after Crowley replied that only a cur would use a knife. He then stabbed George Newell, who had come to Crowley's aid with a club, and James Smith, the 'colored porter' at the Clifton House. In the Journal's account, James Bemis knocked Scott down on the street and took his knife, while a Goshen special to the Indiana State Sentinel said Scott ran three miles into the country before he was caught.

The Sentinel's correspondent reported that a posse was formed 'for the purpose of lynching him' and started in pursuit, but missed the officers, who brought Scott straight to the Goshen jail under strong guard. That night the streets of Elkhart were full of people, and the Journal wrote that the officers had not taken Scott to Goshen 'any too soon.' At Goshen the jail was guarded against an attempt by Crowley's Elkhart friends, whom the Sentinel described as 'thirsting for Scott's blood.'

Crowley, who had received seven stab wounds, died unexpectedly at 10:31 on the morning of August 6. There was talk all that day of organizing a party to go to Goshen and lynch Scott, though the Journal's correspondent expected that 'cooler counsel will probably prevail.'

No report of a party going to Goshen or of an attack on the jail was found. Scott, who was charged with Crowley's murder, claimed he had acted in self-defense, but the Journal said the evidence showed he was the assailant. The coverage does not show an inquest, indictment or trial.

The episode appeared only in white papers, chiefly as an Elkhart stabbing story in which a lynching was expected. The Indianapolis Journal headed its first special 'The Texas Method' and returned to Scott's boasts, writing on August 5 that he would otherwise have 'experienced some of his Texas law.' A wire version that ran in the New York Sun on August 4 under 'A Cowboy Kills Two Men' closed with the line that Scott was expected to be lynched.

Another wire account of the stabbing ran the same day in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Omaha Daily Bee, under headlines that stressed his Texas origin, such as 'Handy With His Knife' and 'He Was From Texas.' Follow-up wire items in the Beatrice Daily Express on August 6 and the Washington Critic on August 7 repeated that he would have been lynched but for the officers and reported the talk of a lynching party under the headline 'A Murderer Worth $100,000.' None of these papers condemned the lynching talk; the Indiana State Sentinel's weekly edition of August 8 carried the only account of the posse's pursuit, headed 'Prisoner Taken to Goshen to Avoid Mob of Lynchers.'

Accounts of the stabbing differ: the Journal placed it in an alley after a quarrel over trespass, while the Sentinel placed it in a butcher's shop and quoted Scott as saying 'all I want is your money.' The Sentinel's special, dated August 3, also spoke of Crowley as already killed, although the Journal and wire reports had him alive until August 6.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Ben Scott
bases: A posse formed in Elkhart to lynch Scott and set out after him, and after Crowley's death there was talk of a party to lynch him at the Goshen jail; no violence against him is reported (A10, A8, A9).

Scott was not killed: officers got him to the Goshen jail before a posse formed to lynch him could reach him, and later talk of a lynching party is not reported to have led to action (A10, A9). The episode is an attempted and threatened lynching, not a completed one.

Independent Indianapolis Journal and Indiana State Sentinel specials and separate wire reports agree that Scott was removed to Goshen to escape lynching and that lynching was threatened (A1, A6, A9, A10, A7, A8); the posse's actual pursuit rests on the Sentinel alone (A10).

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal Elkhart correspondent
accounts.gist: Scott stabbed three men unprovoked in an alley after a trespass quarrel, was disarmed on the street by Bemis, and was removed to Goshen just ahead of local anger; after Crowley died there was talk of a lynching party, but cooler counsel was expected to prevail.

accounts.label: Goshen special to the Indiana State Sentinel
accounts.gist: The quarrel was in a butcher's shop; Scott fled three miles into the country before capture; a posse formed to lynch him started in pursuit but missed the officers, and the Goshen jail was guarded against Crowley's friends.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Scott, a Texan, stabbed three men over trespass; a lynching was expected, and he would have been lynched had officers not been prompt; after Crowley's death there was talk of going to Goshen to lynch him.

accounts.label: Scott's claim
accounts.gist: Scott claimed he acted in self-defense; the Journal said the evidence showed he was the assailant.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal headed its first report 'The Texas Method' and called Scott 'the murderous assailant', describing the lynching talk without endorsing or condemning it and expecting 'cooler counsel' to prevail.
Wire versions ran under headlines such as 'A Cowboy Kills Two Men', 'Handy With His Knife' and 'A Murderer Worth $100,000', presenting a lynching as expected.
The Indiana State Sentinel headed its Goshen special 'Prisoner Taken to Goshen to Avoid Mob of Lynchers' and described Crowley's friends as 'thirsting for Scott's blood'.

Scott's race is not stated in any report; only Smith is described as 'colored'
